subject: geography
title: US Middle School Geography - Culture and Language
subtitle: How culture, language, migration, environment and power shape places and communities
description: A source-faithful human geography pack on culture, language, place, migration, diffusion, diversity, power and sustainability.

data.targetWord: the shared ways of life of a group, including language, beliefs, traditions, values and everyday habits

examples.en-GB: Culture can be seen in food, music, celebrations, buildings and the languages people use.

data.targetWord: a system of spoken, written or signed communication that people use to share ideas and information

examples.en-GB: Language helps people explain places, pass on knowledge and build community identity.

data.targetWord: a regional or group form of a language with distinctive pronunciation, vocabulary or grammar

examples.en-GB: A mountain valley may develop a dialect because people communicate mostly within local communities.

data.targetWord: a way of pronouncing words linked to a person's region, language background or community

examples.en-GB: An accent can give clues about where a speaker has lived or learned a language.

data.targetWord: an area that has one or more shared characteristics, such as climate, language, religion or economy

examples.en-GB: Geographers use regions to compare patterns, but they also look for differences within them.

data.targetWord: an area where people share important cultural traits such as language, religion, foodways or traditions

examples.en-GB: A cultural region may cross national borders if communities share history and language.

data.targetWord: the natural and human-made surroundings of a place, including land, water, climate, buildings and infrastructure

examples.en-GB: The environment can influence housing, transport, farming and daily routines.

data.targetWord: the long-term pattern of weather in a place, including average temperature, rainfall and seasons

examples.en-GB: Climate can affect crops, clothing, housing design and seasonal festivals.

data.targetWord: the short-term condition of the atmosphere, such as today's rain, wind, sunshine or temperature

examples.en-GB: A rainy afternoon is weather, while a wet winter pattern is climate.

data.targetWord: the total number of people living in a place at a particular time

examples.en-GB: A country can have a large population but uneven settlement across its regions.

data.targetWord: the number of people living in a given area, often measured per square mile or kilometre

examples.en-GB: A small city can have high population density if many people live close together.

data.targetWord: something people use from the environment or economy, such as water, soil, forests, money or knowledge

examples.en-GB: Water is a vital resource that can shape settlement patterns and cultural practices.

data.targetWord: the movement of people from one place to another to live, work, study or find safety

examples.en-GB: Migration can bring new languages, foods, businesses and traditions into a city.

data.targetWord: movement into a country from another country, usually to live, work, study or seek safety

examples.en-GB: Immigration can increase language diversity in neighbourhoods, schools and workplaces.

data.targetWord: movement out of a country to live in another country for work, study, family or safety

examples.en-GB: Emigration changes both the place people leave and the place they move to.

data.targetWord: a reason people leave a place, such as conflict, drought, lack of jobs or limited education

examples.en-GB: A drought that reduces farm income can become a push factor for rural families.

data.targetWord: a reason people move to a place, such as jobs, safety, family, education or better services

examples.en-GB: A city with work opportunities and relatives nearby can be a strong pull factor.

data.targetWord: using resources to meet present needs without damaging future generations' ability to meet their own needs

examples.en-GB: Cultural sustainability can include protecting languages, heritage sites and local knowledge.

data.targetWord: the spread of cultural ideas, languages, foods, technologies, beliefs or customs from one place to another

examples.en-GB: Music can spread through social media and then be adapted by local communities.

data.targetWord: the growing connection of people, places, economies, cultures and information across the world

examples.en-GB: Globalisation can spread languages and media while also encouraging local identity protection.

data.targetWord: original peoples of a region whose cultures, languages and histories are connected to that land

examples.en-GB: Indigenous place names can preserve histories and relationships with land and water.

data.targetWord: a language recognised by a government for laws, schools, public services or official communication

examples.en-GB: An official language does not mean every resident uses only that language.

data.targetWord: able to use more than one language, or describing a place where multiple languages are common

examples.en-GB: A multilingual city may need signs, services and schools that support several languages.

data.targetWord: a shared language used by people who do not have the same first language

examples.en-GB: Tok Pisin can act as a lingua franca between language communities in Papua New Guinea.

data.targetWord: a language at risk of disappearing because fewer people, especially children, are learning or using it

examples.en-GB: An endangered language may need schools, media and community programmes to support new speakers.

data.targetWord: the name of a location, often revealing cultural history, language, environment or past events

examples.en-GB: Names such as Mississippi and Chicago show Indigenous language influence in the United States.

data.targetWord: the visible signs of human culture on land, including buildings, roads, signs and settlement patterns

examples.en-GB: A street with bilingual signs and places of worship is part of a cultural landscape.

data.targetWord: the presence of many languages in a place, region or country

examples.en-GB: Language diversity can be high where mountains, islands or migration keep communities distinct.

data.targetWord: the ability to understand and use public information, services and rights in a language people know

examples.en-GB: Language access matters for schools, healthcare, voting and emergency safety.

data.targetWord: decisions by governments or communities about which languages are used, taught, protected or recognised

examples.en-GB: Language planning can affect equality, identity and access to public services.

data.targetWord: a person or group's sense of belonging shaped by language, history, traditions and place

examples.en-GB: Cultural identity may be strengthened by festivals, home language and local stories.

data.targetWord: the process of changing a practice to fit new environments, resources, tastes or community needs

examples.en-GB: A food tradition may adapt when migrants use ingredients available in a new region.

data.targetWord: a landform or natural feature that can limit movement and communication between communities

examples.en-GB: Mountains, forests and islands can act as physical barriers that support language diversity.

data.targetWord: the control and settlement of a place by an outside power, often reshaping language and culture

examples.en-GB: Colonisation often made colonial languages powerful in government, schools and public life.

data.targetWord: a language spoken by a smaller or less politically powerful group within a wider society

examples.en-GB: A minority language may remain strong at home even if another language dominates schools.

data.targetWord: the language with the most public power in government, education, business or media

examples.en-GB: English is dominant in much United States public life even though many home languages are spoken.

data.targetWord: a language people commonly use with family or community members outside official public settings

examples.en-GB: A student may use one home language and another language at school.

data.targetWord: an oversimplified assumption that all people in a group or region are the same

examples.en-GB: Careful geographers avoid stereotypes by describing patterns and exceptions.

data.targetWord: something a map leaves out because it shows selected information rather than complete reality

examples.en-GB: A language map may omit bilingual people, dialects and seasonal migration.

data.targetWord: the skill of reading evidence in tables, graphs or maps to identify patterns and limits

examples.en-GB: Data interpretation helps geographers compare language diversity without treating numbers as perfect.

data.targetWord: community action to increase use of a language that has become less widely spoken

examples.en-GB: Language revival may use immersion schools, media, signs, books and public events.

data.targetWord: protecting cultural knowledge, heritage, language and identity while communities adapt to change

examples.en-GB: Cultural sustainability links heritage protection with social inclusion and environmental care.

data.targetWord: a place where several cultural groups, languages, traditions and identities interact in daily life

examples.en-GB: Ports, border regions and large cities are often multicultural places.

data.targetWord: an area near a political boundary where movement can create bilingual and blended cultural patterns

examples.en-GB: A border region may have signs, schools and businesses using two languages.

data.targetWord: a coastal city linked to other regions through shipping, tourism, finance, universities and travel

examples.en-GB: A port city may hear many languages because trade and migration connect it globally.

data.targetWord: local understanding of seasons, land, water, plants, animals and hazards built through observation

examples.en-GB: Environmental knowledge can help communities manage resources sustainably.

data.targetWord: planning before a hazard so people can understand warnings, reach safety and access support

examples.en-GB: Multilingual alerts and clear maps are important parts of hurricane disaster preparedness.

data.targetWord: the level at which a geographic pattern is studied, such as local, national or global

examples.en-GB: Language patterns may look different at neighbourhood, country and world scales.

Names such as Mississippi, Seattle and Massachusetts show that ____ can reveal history.

data.title: Migration and Cultural Change
data.instruction: Put the cause-and-effect chain in the correct order.
items: A drought reduces farm income in a rural region.
Some families move to a nearby city for work.
New businesses, foods and languages appear in the city.
Schools and services adjust to support multilingual families.
The city's cultural landscape becomes more diverse.

data.title: Language Revival
data.instruction: Put the language revival process in the correct order.
items: A local language has fewer young speakers.
Community members become concerned about language loss.
Schools, families and media programmes create learning opportunities.
More children begin using the language.
The language becomes more visible in signs, events and daily life.

data.title: How Culture Spreads
data.instruction: Put the cultural diffusion process in a logical order.
items: People, goods, ideas or media move between places.
A cultural practice reaches a new community.
Local people adapt the practice to their resources, tastes and needs.
The adapted practice becomes visible in daily life or the cultural landscape.
Geographers study where the pattern appears and why it changed.

data.title: Reading a Language Diversity Data Table
data.instruction: Put these data interpretation steps in order.
items: Identify the countries, regions and approximate language counts in the table.
Look for the highest, lowest and unusual values.
Connect patterns to possible geographic reasons such as islands, mountains or migration.
Remember that language counts are approximate and depend on definitions.
Write a careful conclusion that avoids stereotyping people or regions.
